title: About 90% of Socotra's reptiles occur nowhere else
body: The Socotra Archipelago lies off the Horn of Africa in the northwestern Indian Ocean. UNESCO reports that about 90% of its reptile species and 37% of its plant species are found nowhere else.
takeaway: Protecting an isolated set of islands can preserve lineages with no second home elsewhere on Earth.
source: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Socotra Archipelago (2008)
visual: a small reptile on a rock under a dragon blood tree on Socotra

title: Microbes make dark stripes on Australia's sandstone towers
body: The Bungle Bungle Range in Western Australia has beehive-shaped sandstone towers. Some of their distinctive dark bands are a crust of cyanobacteria, microbes that get energy from light.
takeaway: From a distance, living cells can mark a rocky landscape as clearly as minerals do.
source: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Purnululu National Park (2003)
visual: banded beehive-shaped sandstone towers at Purnululu

title: A bleached coral has lost much of its living colour source
body: Many reef-building corals house tiny algae in their tissues. When heat or other stresses disrupt that partnership, corals can expel the algae, revealing the pale skeleton beneath.
takeaway: A coral can still be alive when it turns white, though losing its partners makes survival harder.
source: NOAA Ocean Service, Are Corals Animals or Plants?
visual: a pale patch on a branching coral beside still-coloured branches

title: Old Faithful's timing depends on its previous eruption
body: Yellowstone's Old Faithful can go about 40 to 100 minutes between eruptions. Shorter eruptions are generally followed by shorter waits, while longer eruptions tend to precede longer ones.
takeaway: The next forecast is based on what the geyser just did, rather than a fixed timetable.
source: US Geological Survey, Old Faithful Geyser
visual: a plume of steam and water above Old Faithful's low rocky mound
